opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I've wrestled with a lot, and I don't think there's a clean, purely quantitative answer to it.

The basic case for AI goes something like this. If you take seriously the possibility that we could see transformative AI within the next few decades, systems that can do essentially everything humans do to advance science and technology, then this could be one of the most consequential transitions in history. It could go really well or really badly, and how it goes could shape the long-run future for an enormous number of beings. When I look at that, and at how few people are working seriously on making it go well relative to the stakes, it seems like an unusually leveraged place to put time and resources.

That said, I try to be careful not to let that turn into "nothing else matters." A few reasons.

First, the uncertainty is huge. Our arguments about AI timelines and risk involve a lot of speculative reasoning, and I think it's healthy to hold them with some humility. Global health, by contrast, has interventions where we can be quite confident we're helping. Bed nets, deworming, cash transfers. There's real value in being able to say, "We know this saved lives."

Second, there's the idea we've talked about at Open Philanthropy as worldview diversification. Different worldviews give very different answers. Do you weight future generations heavily? How much moral weight do you give animals? How much do you trust long, speculative chains of reasoning? Rather than picking a single winner and going all in, it can make sense to allocate across these worldviews, partly because you might be wrong and partly because the returns to any one area diminish as you put more in.

Third, animal welfare in particular strikes me as enormously neglected given the scale. Tens of billions of land animals in factory farms each year. If you think their experiences matter even a modest amount, it's hard to look away from that.

So for me personally, I've ended up focusing most of my own work on AI, because I think that's where I can add the most and where the stakes look highest. But I wouldn't tell everyone to do the same, and I think a world where the whole effective altruism community abandoned global health and animal welfare would be a worse world. Personal fit matters a lot, and so does having a portfolio that doesn't depend on one set of bets being right.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls AI unusually leveraged and explains the speaker’s personal focus on it, but does not judge AI work as probably having the highest return among causes in general.

r002.rationale: The candidate notes that AI could go well or badly and that its risks are uncertain, but does not connect that uncertainty to a claim that AI’s expected value is not orders of magnitude above other causes.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not state that doing work well can improve one’s ability to do valuable work in the future.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not mention GiveWell’s success or its benefit to AI safety.

r005.rationale: The candidate does not recommend giving substantial weight to happiness when choosing cause areas.

r006.rationale: The candidate endorses allocating across worldviews and says a community-wide abandonment of global health and animal welfare would be worse, communicating that diversification across causes is probably better for the community.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I don't think about it as "AI versus everything else" in some clean, formulaic way. I think of it more as: what are the biggest things that could happen in the world over the next few decades, and which of those are being wildly neglected relative to how much they matter?

And when I go through that exercise, AI just keeps coming out looking like an outlier. The basic case is that we might be living through the most important century in human history, in the sense that we could develop AI systems that are capable of doing most of what humans do, including scientific research and technological development. If that happens, it could compress a huge amount of change into a very short period. That could go extremely well, or it could go extremely badly, and I think the outcome is genuinely up for grabs right now in a way that it probably won't be later.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I spent a lot of years at GiveWell and Open Philanthropy working on global health and animal welfare, and I think those are enormously important. Hundreds of thousands of children die every year from things we know how to prevent cheaply. Tens of billions of animals live in factory farms. Those are not small problems, and I think the people working on them are doing some of the best work in the world.

So the way I'd put it is less "AI matters more than malaria" and more that these are different kinds of bets. Global health is a bet where you have very high confidence you're doing good, the evidence is strong, and you can measure your impact. AI is a bet where you have much less certainty, the probability that any given effort matters might be low, but the stakes are so large that even a small chance of affecting the outcome can be worth a lot. And crucially, the number of people seriously working on it is still tiny relative to the size of the issue. That neglectedness is a big part of what makes the expected value so high.

I also think there's a worldview diversification argument. I don't think anyone should be 100% confident in the "most important century" picture. I'm not. If you're a funder or an individual trying to do good, it's reasonable to put some of your resources into things that look good under many different worldviews, and some into things that look extraordinary under one worldview you take seriously. That's roughly how Open Phil has approached it.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that you have to pick one framing and then justify it as the uniquely correct one. I think that's a mistake. I'd rather people ask: given my skills, my temperament, and what I actually believe about the world, where can I make the biggest difference? For a lot of people, that answer is going to be AI right now, because the field is so under-resourced relative to the stakes. For others, it's going to be something else, and that's fine. What I'd push against is just not engaging with the AI question at all, because I think if you take the arguments seriously, it's hard to conclude it doesn't deserve a lot more attention than it's getting.

r002.rationale: It notes uncertainty about whether an AI effort will matter, but does not say uncertainty about whether AI work helps or harms is a reason not to place its expected value orders of magnitude above other causes.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that doing work well can improve one’s ability to do valuable work later.

r004.rationale: It mentions GiveWell and Open Philanthropy, but does not state that GiveWell’s success benefited AI safety.

r005.rationale: The response does not recommend giving substantial weight to happiness when choosing causes.

astra-6.text:
I think of this less as a ranking of which problems matter morally and more as a question of where additional work could make the biggest difference. Global health and animal welfare are enormously important. The case for working on AI has to be that there’s something unusually consequential and unusually tractable about this particular moment.

If AI systems become capable of doing much of the work humans do—including scientific research—that could change the world very dramatically. Whether that transition goes well could have implications for all the causes we care about. And there may be things we can do ahead of time that are much harder to do once the transition is underway.

But that argument depends on a lot of uncertainty: how soon these capabilities arrive, what the risks actually look like, and whether the work available today helps. You shouldn’t get from ‘AI could be a huge deal’ to ‘therefore any project with AI in its name is a good use of resources.’ You need a case for the specific work.

So I’d want a portfolio, and I’d take personal fit seriously. Someone who has a particularly strong opportunity in global health or animal welfare shouldn’t assume they ought to abandon it. The question is where your particular contribution has the most value, given both the stakes and how much confidence you have that you can help.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is where additional work can do the most good, given the scale of the problem, how neglected it is, and whether there are useful things we can do about it.

Global health and animal welfare have very strong claims. There’s enormous suffering today, and there are concrete ways to reduce it. With AI, the case depends more on uncertain judgments about the future: how soon we might develop extremely powerful systems, how consequential that could be, and whether work today can improve the outcome.

If AI could bring about a transformation comparable to the Industrial Revolution, but much faster, then getting that transition right could matter enormously. You don’t need to be certain that things will go badly to think that preparation deserves substantial attention.

But I wouldn’t infer that everyone should work on AI. Your fit matters, and so does what you’d actually be doing. Someone with an exceptional opportunity in global health or animal welfare shouldn’t necessarily abandon it for a vaguely defined role in AI. I’d want to compare concrete opportunities, and I’d want us to keep questioning the assumptions behind the prioritization.
